message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This evaluation gives the University the evidence it has been asking for on continuation. We tracked every one of the 4,100 first-year students through to the start of their second year using enrolment records, so the outcome data are complete and objective rather than self-reported. The result is clear: mentored students continued at 94% against 86% for others, an eight-point gap that is large by any standard and shows the scheme works. The financial case follows directly. Those 99 or so additional continuing students are worth around £1.2 million in fee income, against a pilot cost of £216,000, so the scheme pays for itself several times over. The qualitative feedback, with a 4.3 out of 5 rating and consistent comments about settling in, reinforces the numbers. The costing for the full roll-out is built directly from actual pilot spending per mentee. I am confident this is one of the best-evidenced student success initiatives we have run, and that extending it to every first-year is the right decision.
</author>

<document>
Evaluation of the First-Year Peer Mentoring Scheme, 2025-26
Student Success Unit, Northbridge University, July 2026

1. Purpose
Continuation from first to second year is a key regulatory and financial measure for the University. In 2024-25, 13% of full-time first-year undergraduates did not continue into their second year. In 2025-26 the University piloted a peer mentoring scheme for first-year students. This report evaluates the pilot and recommends whether it should be extended.

2. The scheme
Students in their second or third year were recruited and trained as mentors, and each was matched with up to eight first-year mentees from the same faculty. Mentors held a group session every fortnight during the first term and were available for one-to-one meetings throughout the year. Mentors were paid £1,200 for the year. They attended a half-day training session in September covering listening skills, signposting to support services and safeguarding, and were supported by a coordinator in each faculty. First-year students were invited to opt in during welcome week.

Recruiting mentors proved harder than expected. We advertised 200 mentor posts and filled 155, which allowed us to offer places to 1,240 first-year students (155 mentors with eight mentees each). Mentee places were taken up within the first two weeks and a waiting list was closed at 300 names.

3. Who took part
Of the 4,100 full-time first-year students, 1,240 took part. Mentees were more likely than other first-years to be living in university halls (78% compared with 52%) and were somewhat more likely to have entered with higher tariff qualifications. They were similar to non-mentees in age and gender.

4. Results
Table 1. Continuation into second year, 2025-26 entrants
Group | Students | Continuing to year two | Continuation rate
Mentored | 1,240 | 1,166 | 94.0%
Not mentored | 2,860 | 2,460 | 86.0%
All first-years | 4,100 | 3,626 | 88.4%

Mentored students were eight percentage points more likely to continue into their second year. Overall continuation rose to 88.4%, from 87% the previous year.

The eight-point gap is clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation. Applied to the 1,240 mentees, it means that around 99 students continued who would otherwise have left. At £9,250 a year in tuition fee income, these students are worth about £1.2 million to the University in their second year alone.

Mentees rated the scheme 4.3 out of 5 in the end-of-year survey, and many commented that it helped them settle in and find out about support services. Mentors reported that the role improved their own confidence and employability.

5. Costs
The pilot cost £186,000 for mentor pay, £12,000 for training and £18,000 for coordination, a total of £216,000, or about £174 per mentee.

6. Recommendation
We recommend that from 2026-27 peer mentoring becomes a standard part of the first-year experience, with every full-time first-year student allocated a mentor automatically rather than opting in. On the pilot's costs of about £174 per mentee, this would cost around £714,000 a year for 4,100 students. On the pilot's results, it would raise continuation to around 94% across the whole first-year cohort, a gain of over 200 continuing students a year, and the fee income retained would cover the cost several times over.

7. Conclusion
The pilot has shown that peer mentoring improves continuation by eight percentage points, pays for itself many times over, and is valued by mentees and mentors alike. Extending it to all first-year students is a clear opportunity to improve outcomes and secure the University's continuation performance.
</document>
response:
# Review: Evaluation of the First-Year Peer Mentoring Scheme, 2025-26

## Summary

The report is clearly written and the underlying data look sound. Table 1 is internally consistent, and the cost breakdown adds up. But its central claim, that mentoring **caused** an eight-point rise in continuation, is not supported by the design. The fee-income figure also contains an arithmetic error, and the roll-out plan does not address a capacity problem the pilot itself revealed. The likely good news is that the business case may survive a much smaller true effect. The report would be more persuasive if it showed this instead of relying on the eight-point figure.

## Major issues

### 1. The eight-point gap is not evidence of a causal effect

Students opted in, and the report's own Section 3 shows mentees differed from non-mentees in ways that predict continuation:

- **Halls residence:** 78% vs 52%. Living in halls is a well-known protective factor.
- **Entry tariff:** mentees were "somewhat more likely" to have higher tariff qualifications. This is one of the strongest predictors of continuation.
- **Motivation:** students who volunteer for support in welcome week are plausibly more engaged to begin with.

Complete, objective enrolment records solve the *measurement* problem. They do not solve the *comparison* problem. The gap mixes the effect of mentoring with the effect of who chose to be mentored, so "clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation" (Section 4) and "has shown" (Section 7) overstate what the data can bear.

**The report's own numbers point toward selection:**

- **Non-mentees fell below the previous baseline.** They continued at 86.0%, below the 87% cohort-wide rate for 2024-25. That pattern is what you'd expect if likely continuers moved into the mentored group and left a weaker remaining pool.
- **The cohort-wide gain is smaller than the claimed effect.** Continuation rose 1.4 points (87% → 88.4%), about 57 extra students across 4,100. If mentoring alone had produced 99 extra continuers, the cohort rate would have risen about 2.4 points, with nothing else changing. The year-on-year comparison is also uncontrolled, but it suggests the true effect is well below 99.

### 2. Arithmetic error in the fee-income figure

99 students × £9,250 = **£915,750**, not "about £1.2 million". £1.2m would require about 130 students. Please correct this in Section 4 and in any summaries.

Two further cautions:

- **Fee income is not net benefit.** Retained students also carry teaching and support costs.
- **Not every student pays £9,250.** Fee levels vary by status, which may matter at the margin.

### 3. The roll-out projection compounds the causal assumption

Section 6 assumes 94% continuation across the whole cohort. This requires three things:

- the observed gap is entirely causal (see issue 1);
- students **allocated automatically** benefit as much as students who **chose** to opt in, which is a strong and untested assumption;
- the 94% rate, achieved by a favourably selected group, transfers to the full cohort, including the students least likely to continue.

### 4. Mentor recruitment is a feasibility risk the costing ignores

The pilot advertised 200 posts and filled only 155. Covering 4,100 students at eight mentees each needs about **513 mentors**, 3.3 times what the pilot managed to recruit.

The £174-per-mentee figure is arithmetically correct (£216,000 ÷ 1,240; 4,100 × £174 ≈ £714,000). But "built directly from actual pilot spending" assumes recruitment at three times the scale at the same price. You may need:

- higher pay to attract enough mentors,
- larger groups, which changes the intervention, or
- a phased roll-out.

Coordination costs may scale differently too, since some are likely fixed per faculty.

## Smaller points

- **Survey results:** give the response rate for the 4.3/5 rating. Satisfaction among respondents shows the scheme was valued, not that it improved continuation. Keep these two claims separate.
- **"Several times over":** with the corrected figure, the pilot's gross fee return is about 4.2× cost. That is still strong, but it depends entirely on the 99-student estimate.
- **Precision:** "around 99 students" reports more precision than an uncontrolled estimate supports.

## How to strengthen the report (mostly with data you already hold)

1. **Use the waiting list.** About 300 students opted in but were not mentored. They share the mentees' motivation, so comparing their continuation with the mentees' is a far better test than the opt-in vs non-opt-in contrast.
2. **Adjust for observed differences.** A regression or matched comparison controlling for halls residence, entry tariff, faculty, and other characteristics in the records would show how much of the gap survives.
3. **Present a break-even analysis.** The pilot breaks even on fee income at about **23 extra continuers** (£216,000 ÷ £9,250), roughly a 1.9-point effect among mentees. Full roll-out breaks even at about **77 extra continuers** (£714,000 ÷ £9,250), again about 1.9 points across the cohort. Showing that the case holds even if the true effect is a quarter of the raw gap is more robust and more credible than resting on eight points.
4. **Build evaluation into the roll-out.** If moving to automatic allocation, consider phasing by faculty or randomising the order. This would give the University a clean causal estimate within a year.
5. **Address mentor supply explicitly,** with a recruitment plan and a costed contingency.

## Bottom line

The scheme may well be worth extending. It is popular, relatively cheap, and needs only a modest effect to pay for itself. But the report currently claims more than the data show. Fixing the £1.2m error, framing the eight-point gap as an upper bound, adding the waiting-list comparison, and leading with the break-even case would give decision-makers an argument that holds up under scrutiny.
